mainTopic: How a מחאה (protest) against someone holding land works: secrecy, protesting when the occupant is absent, and how many must hear it
overview: An owner makes a מחאה (protest) against the person living on his land so that the occupant cannot build a חזקה. A protest only works if word of it can reach the occupant. The גמרא first asks what happens when the owner or the witnesses say they will keep it quiet. רב זביד says 'don't tell him' ruins the protest, and רב פפא says it does not, because 'your friend has a friend'. When total silence is promised, both say the protest fails, but רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע says people repeat things they are not really bound to hide. Next, רבא quotes רב נחמן that a מחאה counts even when the occupant is not there. רבא challenges this from רבי יהודה's three-year timeline, and the גמרא answers that coming home is just good advice. It also explains that רבא accepted the rule after hearing it from רב נחמן. Finally, two students report רבי יוחנן as requiring two or three listeners for a מחאה, and the גמרא begins tying this to a rule of רבה בר רב הונא that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A protest that promises a future court case is valid
steps.stepSummary: The protest formula ends with 'tomorrow I will claim him in court', and such a protest counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: '...and tomorrow I will sue him in court.' This counts as a protest.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes describing a proper מחאה. If the owner says he will take the occupant to court in the future, this counts as a valid protest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line ends a statement that started before our text. The owner announces his claim and says he plans to go to court, so this is a real מחאה. The rest of the section asks what happens when secrecy is added to it.

keyTerms.meaning: A protest. The owner formally announces that the person living on his land has no right to it.
I will claim / I will sue
In court
Tomorrow. Here it means 'in the future'.

phrases.english: and tomorrow I will claim from him in court
it is a protest.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָוְיָא מֶחָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the discussion of valid protest wording that started earlier on the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A protest that says the owner will sue the occupant in court is a valid מחאה.

steps.title: What if the protester says 'Don't tell him'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a protest still counts if the owner tells the witnesses not to tell the occupant.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said, 'Don't tell him,' what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new case. The owner protests but tells the witnesses, 'Don't tell him.' This question sets up the argument that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A protest is supposed to warn the occupant so he keeps his proof safe. If the owner himself asks for secrecy, maybe the warning will never reach the occupant. The question is whether that cancels the protest.

keyTerms.meaning: Don't tell him
What? Here: what is the law?

phrases.english: If he said, 'Do not tell him,' what is the law?
phrases.notes: 'He' is the owner who is protesting. 'Him' is the person living on the land.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר ״לָא תֵּימְרוּ לֵיהּ״, מַאי?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the valid protest and adds a request for secrecy.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a protest still count if the protester tells the witnesses not to tell the occupant?

steps.title: רב זביד: The protest fails because he asked for secrecy
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד says the protest does not count, since the owner himself said not to tell.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said: He said 'Don't tell him!' So it is not a protest.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד answers that this is not a valid מחאה. The owner's own words show that he did not want the occupant to find out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב זביד reads 'Don't tell him' as a full request for secrecy. If no one tells the occupant, the protest cannot do its job of warning him. So it does not count.

keyTerms.meaning: But he is saying...! This points to the person's own words as proof.

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said:
But he is saying, 'Do not tell him!'
phrases.notes: He means: so the word won't reach the occupant, and the protest doesn't count.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב זְבִיד: הָא קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Not a valid protest, because the owner asked that the occupant not be told.

steps.title: רב פפא: 'Don't tell him' means tell others, so word will spread
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says the owner only meant not to tell the occupant directly. Others will be told, and word will reach him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: He meant, 'Don't tell him himself, but tell other people.' Your friend has a friend, and your friend's friend has a friend.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא disagrees with רב זביד. He reads 'Don't tell him' narrowly: don't go to the occupant yourselves, but you may tell other people. News travels, so the protest is valid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument is about what the owner's words mean. רב פפא says the owner only blocked direct telling. Once other people hear, the news passes from friend to friend until it reaches the occupant.

keyTerms.meaning: To him himself
To others
Your friend has a friend. In other words, news spreads.

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that a מחאה does not have to be told to the occupant directly. It only has to be likely to reach him.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
to him himself do not tell it,
to others, tell them;
your friend has a friend,
and your friend's friend has a friend.
phrases.notes: In other words, the news gets passed along until it reaches the occupant, so the protest counts.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר: לְדִידֵיהּ לָא תֵּימְרוּ לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב זביד's reading of the owner's words.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Valid protest. The owner only blocked telling the occupant directly, and word will reach him through others.

steps.title: What if the witnesses say 'We won't tell him'?
steps.stepSummary: A new case: this time the witnesses say they will not tell the occupant.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they said to him, 'We will not tell him,' what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא flips the case. Now the witnesses, not the owner, say they will not tell the occupant. This sets up the same argument again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the last case, the owner asked for secrecy. Here, the witnesses say on their own that they will keep quiet. Will word still reach the occupant?

keyTerms.meaning: We will not tell him

phrases.english: If they said to him, 'We will not tell him,'
phrases.notes: 'They' are the witnesses who heard the protest. 'To him' is the owner. The question 'what is the law?' is understood but not written.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: ״לָא אָמְרִינַן לֵיהּ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same kind of case as step 2, but now the witnesses are the ones promising to stay quiet.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a protest count if the witnesses say they will not tell the occupant?

steps.title: רב זביד: The witnesses' refusal ruins the protest
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד says it is not a valid protest, because the witnesses said they won't tell.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said: They said, 'We will not tell him!' So it is not a protest.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד stays with his view. If the witnesses say they will not tell, the protest does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His reasoning is the same as before. If the people who heard the protest will not pass it on, it will not reach the occupant. So the protest fails.

keyTerms.meaning: But they are saying to him...!

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said:

phrases.aramaic: הָא קָא אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ ״לָא אָמְרִינַן לֵיהּ״!
phrases.english: But they are saying to him, 'We will not tell him!'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב זְבִיד: הָא קָא אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 5, using the same reasoning as step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Not a valid protest, because the witnesses said they won't tell.

steps.title: רב פפא: They meant they won't tell him directly, but news spreads
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא again says the words only rule out telling the occupant directly. Others will hear, so the protest is valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: They meant, 'We won't tell him himself, but we will tell others.' Your friend has a friend, and your friend's friend has a friend.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא uses the same reasoning for the witnesses. They only said they will not go to the occupant themselves. They will still talk to others, so word will reach him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both רב זביד and רב פפא are consistent across the two cases. The only question is how far the words 'not tell him' reach. רב פפא says they only mean 'not directly'.

keyTerms.meaning: They tell them / we tell them

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
to him himself we will not tell it,
but to others we will tell;
your friend has a friend,
and your friend's friend has a friend.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר: לְדִידֵיהּ לָא אָמְרִינַן לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב זביד in step 6, the same way as step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Valid protest. The witnesses will tell others, and the news will reach the occupant.
steps.whatToRemember: In both 'don't tell him' cases, רב זביד says the protest fails. רב פפא says it works, because 'not him' still allows telling others, and news spreads.

steps.title: What if the protester says 'Don't let a word out'?
steps.stepSummary: A stronger case: the owner tells the witnesses not to let even a word out.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said to them, 'Don't let a word come out from you,' what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks about a stronger secrecy request. The owner tells the witnesses not to say a word to anyone. This sets up the next ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Don't tell him' could still allow telling others. 'Don't let a word out' seems to forbid telling anyone at all. So רב פפא's answer of 'tell others' may no longer work here.

keyTerms.meaning: A word / a bit of talk
Let it not come out from you

phrases.english: If he said to them, 'Let not a word come out from you,'
phrases.notes: The owner is speaking to the witnesses. This time he is asking for total silence, not just 'don't tell him'.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ: ״לָא תִּיפּוֹק לְכוּ שׁוּתָא״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Makes the secrecy request in step 2 stronger.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a protest count if the owner asks for total silence?

steps.title: רב זביד: With 'not a word', the protest fails
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד says the protest does not count, since the owner asked for total silence.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said: He said, 'Don't let a word out!' So it is not a protest.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד rules that this protest is not valid. The owner told them to say nothing to anyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If רב זביד already said the protest fails with 'don't tell him', it surely fails here. רב פפא does not argue with him in this case, which hints that he agrees.

keyTerms.meaning: He is saying

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said:
But he is saying, 'Let not a word come out from you!'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב זְבִיד: הָא קָאָמַר ״לָא תִּיפּוֹק לְכוּ שׁוּתָא״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Not a valid protest, because the owner asked for complete silence.

steps.title: What if the witnesses say 'We won't let a word out'?
steps.stepSummary: The matching case: the witnesses promise to say nothing at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they said to him, 'We will not let a word out,' what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the witness version of the 'not a word' case. The witnesses promise total silence. This sets up רב פפא's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the stronger form of step 5. If the witnesses will tell no one at all, then 'your friend has a friend' seems not to apply.

keyTerms.meaning: We will not let out

phrases.english: If they said to him, 'We will not let a word out,'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: ״לָא מַפְּקִינַן שׁוּתָא״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The witness version of step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a protest count if the witnesses promise total silence?

steps.title: רב פפא: With 'not a word', even he says the protest fails
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא agrees that when the witnesses promise total silence, the protest does not count.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: They said, 'We will not let a word out!' So it is not a protest.
steps.whatsHappening: Now רב פפא rules that the protest fails. The witnesses promised to say nothing to anyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, רב פפא saved the protest because the witnesses could still tell others. 'Not a word' closes off that option, so his own reasoning leads to 'not valid'. In the 'not a word' cases, רב זביד and רב פפא agree.

keyTerms.meaning: They are saying

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רב פפא changed his mind. He always said the protest works because others will be told. Here the witnesses promise to tell no one, so his reason no longer applies.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
But they are saying to him, 'We will not let a word out!'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: הָא קָאָמְרִי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 10. Shows that רב פפא's lenient view in step 7 had a limit.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Not a valid protest, because the witnesses promised total silence.

steps.title: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע: People repeat things they weren't really bound to hide
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע says that even 'not a word' does not ruin the protest. A secret a person is not truly responsible for keeping gets told without his noticing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא son of רב יהושע said: Anything that a person is not truly burdened with keeping secret, he ends up saying without even realizing it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע disagrees with the rulings in steps 9 and 11. He says that even with a promise of total silence, the protest still works, because people end up talking anyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He looks at how people really behave. Nothing actually requires the witnesses to keep this secret. So even if they promise silence, they will mention it without thinking, and word will reach the occupant. A promise of secrecy does not cancel a מחאה.

keyTerms.meaning: A matter / a thing
Placed upon him; something he is truly burdened with
And not on purpose; without realizing it

steps.whatToRemember: There are three views. רב זביד: any request or promise not to tell ruins the protest. רב פפא: only 'not a word' ruins it. רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע: even 'not a word' does not ruin it, because people talk without noticing.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the גמרא judges whether a protest works by how people actually behave, not only by the exact words they used.

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אָמַר:
phrases.english: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua said:

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל מִילְּתָא דְלָא רַמְיָא עֲלֵיהּ דְּאִינִישׁ,
phrases.english: any matter that is not placed upon a person as a duty,
phrases.notes: He means a secret the person isn't truly responsible for keeping.

phrases.english: he says it without being aware of it.
phrases.notes: So the news will reach the occupant anyway, and the protest counts.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אָמַר: כֹּל מִילְּתָא דְלָא רַמְיָא עֲלֵיהּ דְּאִינִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the 'not valid' rulings of steps 9 and 11 using a general rule about how people behave.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The rulings of רב זביד and רב פפא that a promise of total silence cancels the protest.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: They assume people keep secrets they promised to keep. In reality, people repeat things they are not truly bound to hide, so word reaches the occupant.

steps.title: A protest made when the possessor is absent still counts
steps.stepSummary: רבא quotes רב נחמן: a מחאה made when the מחזיק is not present is a valid מחאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said in the name of רב נחמן: a protest made when the possessor is not there is still a protest.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new rule: the owner can protest even when the person living on his land is not there to hear it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier steps discussed whether the מחאה reaches the מחזיק through the witnesses. Here רב נחמן says outright that the מחזיק does not have to be present. A מחאה made in front of others still counts.

keyTerms.meaning: A protest: the owner announces that someone is living on his land without the right to.
Not in his presence, meaning the מחזיק is not there.
Is, counts as.

steps.whyThisMatters: This rule protects an owner who is far away. He can still stop the other person's חזקה from forming.

phrases.english: Rava said that Rav Nachman said:
A protest made not in his presence is a valid protest.
phrases.notes: "His presence" means the person who is living on and using the field.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new statement about מחאה that is not made in front of the מחזיק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A מחאה made when the מחזיק is absent is valid.

steps.title: Why does the owner need to come home if he could protest from afar?
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges רב נחמן from רבי יהודה, who builds the three years around the owner traveling back from אספמיא. If a distant מחאה counts, why travel at all?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא challenged רב נחמן. רבי יהודה said: they set three years so that if the owner is in Spain and someone holds his land for one year, people go and tell him during the next year, and he comes back in the year after that. If a protest made when the possessor is absent counts, why does he need to come? Let him stay where he is and protest!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks רב נחמן's rule using רבי יהודה's explanation of why חזקה takes three years.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה's timeline has the owner come home in the third year. That suggests he must be present to stop the חזקה. If he could protest far away, the trip back would be pointless, so רב נחמן's rule seems wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: Spain: an example of a faraway place.
If it enters your mind: if you really thought so.
Let him protest.

phrases.english: Rava challenged Rav Nachman:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה: לֹא אָמְרוּ שָׁלֹשׁ שָׁנִים,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda said: they only said three years
phrases.notes: The three years are the time needed for a חזקה, from the משנה.

phrases.english: so that if the owner is in Spain
and the other person holds the land for a year,
people will go and tell the owner during the next year,
and he will come back in the following year.
And if you think
that a protest not in his presence is a valid protest,
why do I need him to come?
Let him stay there in his place and protest!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב נחמן's rule from step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's rule that a מחאה made when the מחזיק is absent is valid.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יהודה requires the owner to travel home. That travel only makes sense if a distant מחאה does not work.

steps.title: Coming home is just good advice
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי יהודה was giving practical advice: come home so you can actually take back the land and its produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, he is teaching us good advice: that the owner should come and take back the land and the produce.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב נחמן by saying the trip home is not required to make the מחאה work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A distant מחאה does stop the חזקה. But a מחאה alone does not get the owner his field back. רבי יהודה advises him to come so he can go to court and take back the land and its fruits.

keyTerms.meaning: Good advice: a practical tip, not a legal requirement.
He is teaching us.
The land and the produce.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as saying the owner must come home for the מחאה to count. Coming home is advice, not a condition.

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם עֵצָה טוֹבָה קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן,
phrases.english: There, he is teaching us good advice:
that he should come and take the land and the produce.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם עֵצָה טוֹבָה קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets the source: the trip home is advice, not a legal requirement.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owner must come home for his מחאה to count.
steps.terutzMaskana: A distant מחאה counts. Coming home is only so he can actually take back the land and its produce.

steps.title: רבא contradicts himself?
steps.stepSummary: Since רבא challenged the rule, he seems to disagree with it. But elsewhere רבא himself says this exact rule!
steps.simpleTranslation: Since רבא challenged רב נחמן, that shows he does not hold that a protest not in his presence counts. But רבא himself said: a protest not in his presence is a valid protest!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices a contradiction in רבא: he argues against the rule, yet he also states it as his own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who raises a challenge usually disagrees with the rule. Yet a statement of רבא supports the same rule. So which does רבא really hold?

keyTerms.meaning: From the fact that he challenges.
It follows, it can be inferred.
But didn't he say?: the word that brings in a contradiction.

phrases.aramaic: מִדְּקָא מוֹתֵיב לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַב נַחְמָן –
phrases.english: From the fact that Rava challenged Rav Nachman,
it follows that he does not hold
that a protest not in his presence is a valid protest.
But didn't Rava say:
A protest not in his presence is a valid protest!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִדְּקָא מוֹתֵיב לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the challenge in step 14 to show a contradiction in רבא's own view.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא challenged the rule, so he seems to reject it. But he is also quoted stating it.

steps.title: רבא accepted it after hearing it from רב נחמן
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenged the rule at first. After hearing רב נחמן's answer, he accepted it.
steps.simpleTranslation: After he heard it from רב נחמן, he agreed with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves the contradiction by putting the two things in time order: challenge first, agreement later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no real contradiction. רבא's challenge came before he was convinced. Once he heard רב נחמן's teaching, he took it on and repeated it himself.

keyTerms.meaning: After.
That he heard it.
He held it, agreed with it.

steps.whatToRemember: The rule stands: a מחאה made when the מחזיק is absent is valid, and רבא agrees with it in the end.

phrases.english: After he heard it from Rav Nachman, he held it.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּתַר דְּשַׁמְעַהּ מֵרַב נַחְמָן, סַבְרַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Time order: he challenged first and accepted later.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא rejects the rule because he challenged it.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבא accepted the rule after hearing it from רב נחמן.

steps.title: How many people must hear a protest?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא meets the students of רבי יוחנן and asks: did רבי יוחנן say how many people must be present for a מחאה?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא met רבי יוחנן's students. He said to them: did רבי יוחנן say how many people a protest must be made in front of?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question begins: how many listeners does a valid מחאה need?
steps.deeperAnalysis: We now know the מחזיק does not have to be there. So who does have to hear it? רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא wants רבי יוחנן's number.

keyTerms.meaning: He found them, met them.
His students.
With how many: in front of how many people.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Chanina found
the students of Rabbi Yochanan.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: מִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
phrases.english: He said to them: Did Rabbi Yochanan say
in front of how many a protest must be made?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַשְׁכְּחִינְהוּ רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא לְתַלְמִידָיו דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question about how many people must hear a מחאה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The number of people a מחאה must be made in front of, according to רבי יוחנן.

steps.title: Two reports: two people or three people
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר אבא reports that רבי יוחנן said two people. רבי אבהו reports that רבי יוחנן said three.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: a protest is made in front of two. רבי אבהו said in the name of רבי יוחנן: a protest is made in front of three.
steps.whatsHappening: The question gets two different answers, both quoted from רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two students remember רבי יוחנן differently. One says two people are enough, and the other says three are needed. This sets up the גמרא's search for the reason behind the difference.

keyTerms.meaning: In front of two people.
In front of three people.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
A protest is made in front of two.
Rabbi Abbahu said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
A protest is made in front of three.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 18 with two different reports.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: One report says two people; the other says three people.

steps.title: Do they argue about רבה בר רב הונא's rule?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to suggest that the two reports argue about a rule of רבה בר רב הונא, which starts with something said in front of three people.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say they argue about the rule of רבה בר רב הונא? For רבה בר רב הונא said: anything that is said in front of three people...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It suggests a reason for the two-or-three argument by bringing in רבה בר רב הונא's rule, which continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא tries to tie the number three to a known rule about things said in front of three people. The full rule, and whether the suggestion holds, come on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say?: the word that brings in a suggestion the גמרא is testing.
They argue.
In front of three people.

steps.confusionAlert: This line stops in the middle of a sentence. The rest of רבה בר רב הונא's rule continues on the next amud.

phrases.aramaic: לֵימָא בִּדְרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא קָא מִיפַּלְגִי –
phrases.english: Shall we say they argue about the rule of Rabba bar Rav Huna?
For Rabba bar Rav Huna said:
Any matter that is said in front of three people,

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא בִּדְרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא קָא מִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Suggests a reason behind the two reports of step 19.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the two-or-three argument depends on רבה בר רב הונא's rule about things said in front of three.
